section: Introduction
label: External conditions alone cannot explain complex coadaptations
measurable_quantities: magnitude of phenotypic plasticity induced by environment versus heritable trait differences; degree of trait matching between interacting species
candidate_data: Common-garden and reciprocal-transplant studies of plasticity versus heritable divergence; interaction-network data such as the Web of Life database.

section: Introduction
label: Overproduction plus slight profitable variation leads to natural selection
measurable_quantities: offspring produced versus offspring surviving to reproduce; association between heritable trait values and survival or reproductive success
candidate_data: Life-table and demographic data (COMADRE, COMPADRE), long-term individual-based field studies of selection, and experimental-evolution datasets such as the LTEE.

section: Introduction
label: Natural selection causes extinction of less improved forms and divergence
measurable_quantities: extinction rates of lineages; morphological disparity among descendant lineages over time
candidate_data: Fossil occurrence and extinction data (Paleobiology Database) and time-calibrated phylogenies (TimeTree, Open Tree of Life) with trait data.

section: Introduction
label: Species are not immutable but descend from other, mostly extinct, species
measurable_quantities: phylogenetic relatedness of congeneric species; presence of extinct ancestral or stem taxa in the fossil record
candidate_data: Molecular phylogenies and divergence times (Open Tree of Life, TimeTree, GenBank) combined with fossil occurrences (Paleobiology Database).

section: Introduction
label: Natural selection is the main but not exclusive means of modification
measurable_quantities: proportion of phenotypic or sequence divergence attributable to selection versus other processes; strength of selection on traits in wild populations
candidate_data: Compilations of selection gradients in wild populations, genome-wide scans for selection in GenBank/SRA data, and experimental-evolution results such as the LTEE.

section: Causes of Variability
label: Domesticated forms vary more among individuals than wild species do
measurable_quantities: within-breed or within-variety phenotypic variance; within-population phenotypic variance in wild relatives
candidate_data: Morphometric and trait datasets for breeds and their wild progenitors (e.g. TRY plant trait database for crops and wild relatives) and genomic variation data in GenBank/SRA.

section: Causes of Variability
label: Greater domestic variability is caused by changed, less uniform conditions
measurable_quantities: phenotypic variance of populations raised under novel versus ancestral conditions; heritable variance generated per generation under changed conditions
candidate_data: Experimental-evolution and stress-induced variation studies (e.g. Dryad experimental-evolution datasets) and common-garden comparisons of crops and wild relatives.

section: Causes of Variability
label: Variability arises mainly from effects on reproductive elements before conception
measurable_quantities: offspring variance as a function of parental environmental exposure before conception; fertility under confinement or cultivation
candidate_data: Parental-environment and germline mutation-rate studies with sequencing data in GenBank/SRA; zoo breeding records such as those in ZIMS (Species360).

section: Effects of Habit
label: Inherited effects of use and disuse modify domestic animals
measurable_quantities: relative wing and leg bone mass in domestic versus wild ducks; trait differences in offspring of exercised versus unexercised parents
candidate_data: Museum osteological collections (e.g. records accessible via GBIF and VertNet) for the morphological pattern; transgenerational experiments for the claimed cause.

section: Correlation of Growth
label: Selecting one trait unconsciously modifies other correlated parts
measurable_quantities: correlated responses of unselected traits in selection experiments; genetic correlations between traits
candidate_data: Artificial-selection experiment datasets (e.g. the Illinois long-term maize selection experiment, mouse and Drosophila selection lines on Dryad) and AnimalQTLdb.

section: Inheritance
label: Inherited peculiarities appear in offspring at the age they appeared in parent
measurable_quantities: age of onset of heritable traits or diseases in parents and offspring
candidate_data: Pedigree databases of age of onset for heritable conditions, e.g. OMIA (Online Mendelian Inheritance in Animals) and OMIM.

section: Character of Domestic Varieties
label: Domestic races differ like congeneric species, but usually less
measurable_quantities: morphological distance between breeds of one species; morphological distance between congeneric wild species
candidate_data: Morphometric datasets of breeds (e.g. dog and pigeon skull morphometrics on Dryad) compared with wild-species trait data from museum collections accessible via GBIF.

section: Origin of Domestic Varieties from one or more Species
label: Any wild species domesticated as long would vary as much as existing domestics
measurable_quantities: standing genetic and phenotypic variation in domesticated progenitors versus non-domesticated relatives; rate of phenotypic diversification under captive breeding
candidate_data: Long-term captive-domestication experiments (e.g. the Novosibirsk farm-fox experiment) and genomic diversity data for wild species in GenBank/SRA.

section: Origin of Domestic Varieties from one or more Species
label: Domestic dogs descend from several wild species
measurable_quantities: genomic ancestry proportions of dog breeds from wild canid species; phylogenetic placement of dogs among Canidae
candidate_data: Modern and ancient canid genome sequences in GenBank/SRA and the European Nucleotide Archive.

section: Domestic Pigeons, their Differences and Origin
label: All domestic pigeon breeds descend from the rock-pigeon
measurable_quantities: genomic ancestry of pigeon breeds; phylogenetic relationships of breeds to wild Columba species
candidate_data: Whole-genome resequencing data for pigeon breeds and wild Columba in GenBank/SRA.

section: Principle of Selection anciently followed, its Effects
label: Domestic breeds arise mainly by man's accumulation of successive variations
measurable_quantities: cumulative response to selection over generations; historical trait trajectories of breeds and cultivars
candidate_data: Long-term artificial-selection experiments (e.g. the Illinois long-term maize selection experiment) and breed-history genomic data in GenBank/SRA.

section: Principle of Selection anciently followed, its Effects
label: Races differ most in the parts man selects
measurable_quantities: among-variety variance in the selected organ; among-variety variance in unselected organs
candidate_data: Crop germplasm trait records (e.g. USDA GRIN-Global germplasm evaluation data) and TRY plant trait database.

section: Methodical and Unconscious Selection
label: Unconscious selection over centuries modifies any breed
measurable_quantities: change in breed traits over historical time; trait differences between historical and modern specimens of a breed
candidate_data: Ancient-DNA and archaeozoological time series of domestic animals and crops, and historical breed-standard morphometrics.

section: Unknown Origin of our Domestic Productions
label: Slow accumulated change hides the wild parents of old cultivated plants
measurable_quantities: morphological divergence of crops from wild progenitors; duration of cultivation
candidate_data: Crop wild relative inventories and phylogenomic data on crop origins (GenBank/SRA, Crop Wild Relatives inventory of the Crop Trust), with archaeobotanical dates.

section: Methodical and Unconscious Selection
label: Domestic races differ greatly externally but little internally
measurable_quantities: among-breed variance in external traits; among-breed variance in internal organ size and structure
candidate_data: Breed morphometric and anatomical datasets (e.g. dog and chicken breed studies on Dryad) and AnimalQTLdb trait records.

section: Circumstances favourable to Man’s power of Selection
label: Keeping large numbers of individuals favours successful selection
measurable_quantities: response to selection as a function of population size; number of novel variants per generation versus population size
candidate_data: Selection experiments varying population size (Drosophila and mouse selection lines on Dryad) and experimental-evolution data such as the LTEE.

section: Summary
label: Accumulative selection is the predominant cause of change in domestic races
measurable_quantities: fraction of breed differentiation attributable to selection versus drift, admixture or plasticity
candidate_data: Genome-wide selection scans and admixture analyses of breeds and crops using GenBank/SRA data.

section: Individual Differences
label: Individual differences supply the material for natural selection
measurable_quantities: heritability of individual trait differences in wild populations; response to natural selection in wild populations
candidate_data: Long-term wild pedigree studies and compilations of heritability and selection estimates; experimental-evolution datasets on Dryad.

section: Individual Differences
label: Polymorphic genera vary in traits of no use, unfixed by selection
measurable_quantities: fitness effects of the variable characters; within-genus variability of characters compared with non-polymorphic genera
candidate_data: Taxonomic and trait data for apomictic plant complexes (World Flora Online, TRY plant trait database) with field fitness measurements.

section: Doubtful species
label: Doubtful forms of mobile animals are rare within a country but common between areas
measurable_quantities: number of contested species/subspecies pairs that are sympatric versus allopatric
candidate_data: Comparison of differing taxonomies (e.g. Clements/eBird, IOC World Bird List, HBW and BirdLife checklists) with range maps from BirdLife International and GBIF occurrences.

section: Doubtful species
label: No clear line separates species, sub-species, varieties and individual differences
measurable_quantities: distribution of genetic or morphological distances among infraspecific and interspecific pairs; frequency of taxonomic disagreement over rank
candidate_data: Sequence divergence data such as DNA barcodes in BOLD and GenBank, and taxonomic checklists with infraspecific ranks (WCVP, Catalogue of Life).

section: Doubtful species
label: Natural selection turns slight varieties into more distinct ones and species
measurable_quantities: divergence between incipient species over time; signatures of divergent selection between populations
candidate_data: Population-genomic data for speciation continua in GenBank/SRA and divergence-time estimates in TimeTree.

section: Doubtful species
label: The term species is arbitrary and not essentially different from variety
candidate_data: none known

section: Wide ranging, much diffused, and common species vary most
label: Dominant species, widespread and abundant, produce the most varieties
measurable_quantities: number of recorded varieties or subspecies per species; geographic range size; local abundance or occupancy
candidate_data: Infraspecific taxon counts from the World Checklist of Vascular Plants (WCVP) or POWO combined with range and occurrence data from GBIF.

section: Species of the larger genera in any country vary more than the species of the smaller genera
label: Species of larger genera more often present varieties
measurable_quantities: proportion of species with recorded varieties by genus size; mean number of varieties per varying species by genus size
candidate_data: Genus sizes and infraspecific taxa from the World Checklist of Vascular Plants (WCVP) or regional floras, and the Catalogue of Life for beetles.

section: Species of the larger genera in any country vary more than the species of the smaller genera
label: Small genera often grow large while large genera peak, decline and vanish
measurable_quantities: species richness of genera through time; genus duration and trajectory of richness before extinction
candidate_data: Fossil occurrence data from the Paleobiology Database.

section: Species of the larger genera in any country vary more than the species of the smaller genera
label: Where many species of a genus have formed, many are still forming
measurable_quantities: recent speciation rate per clade; clade species richness
candidate_data: Time-calibrated phylogenies (Open Tree of Life, TimeTree) for estimating tip speciation rates against clade richness.

section: Many of the species of the larger genera resemble varieties in being very closely, but unequally, related to each other, and in having restricted ranges
label: Species in large genera differ from one another by small amounts
measurable_quantities: mean pairwise morphological or genetic distance among congeners as a function of genus size
candidate_data: Sequence data (GenBank, BOLD) and trait data (TRY plant trait database) analysed against genus sizes from WCVP or Catalogue of Life.

section: Many of the species of the larger genera resemble varieties in being very closely, but unequally, related to each other, and in having restricted ranges
label: Species of large genera cluster unequally around certain species
measurable_quantities: phylogenetic tree balance and clustering of species within genera; variance of pairwise distances among congeners
candidate_data: Species-level phylogenies from Open Tree of Life and TimeTree, and GenBank sequence data.

section: Many of the species of the larger genera resemble varieties in being very closely, but unequally, related to each other, and in having restricted ranges
label: Species very closely allied to others have restricted ranges, like varieties
measurable_quantities: range size of species as a function of genetic or morphological distance to nearest relative; range size of varieties versus their parent species
candidate_data: Occurrence data from GBIF and range maps combined with phylogenies from Open Tree of Life or GenBank sequence data.

section: Summary
label: Analogies between species of large genera and varieties support descent
candidate_data: none known

section: Summary
label: Larger genera tend to grow larger and dominant forms more dominant
measurable_quantities: correlation between clade size and diversification rate; number of descendant species from widespread versus restricted ancestors
candidate_data: Time-calibrated phylogenies (Open Tree of Life, TimeTree) and fossil genus richness trajectories in the Paleobiology Database.

section: Geometrical powers of increase
label: Overproduction makes a struggle for existence inevitable
measurable_quantities: intrinsic rate of increase; fecundity; proportion of offspring surviving to reproduce; population growth rate over time
candidate_data: Demographic life-table databases such as COMPADRE and COMADRE, AnAge life-history data, and long-term population time series such as the Global Population Dynamics Database.

section: Rapid increase of naturalised animals and plants
label: Geometrical increase explains rapid spread of naturalised species
measurable_quantities: population growth rate of introduced species after arrival; range expansion rate; fecundity in native versus introduced range; juvenile survival in native versus introduced range
candidate_data: Naturalised-flora and invasion databases (GloNAF, GBIF occurrence time series) combined with native-versus-introduced range demographic comparisons in the published literature.

section: Geometrical powers of increase
label: Average abundance depends only indirectly on fecundity
measurable_quantities: clutch size or seed output per individual; population abundance or density; early-life mortality rate; parental care
candidate_data: Life-history trait compilations (AnAge, AVONET, TRY plant traits, FishBase) combined with abundance estimates (e.g. global bird population estimates, BioTIME, GBIF).

section: Nature of the checks to increase
label: Predation, more often than food supply, sets average numbers
measurable_quantities: population density with and without predator removal; population response to food supplementation; predation mortality rate
candidate_data: Predator-removal and food-supplementation field experiments compiled in meta-analyses (data often deposited in Dryad), and long-term predator-prey time series such as the Global Population Dynamics Database.

section: Effects of climate
label: Periodic extreme cold or drought is the most effective check
measurable_quantities: population change across extreme climatic events; mortality during severe winters or droughts; relative contribution of climate versus biotic factors to population fluctuations
candidate_data: Long-term bird monitoring (North American Breeding Bird Survey, Pan-European Common Bird Monitoring Scheme), BioTIME and Living Planet Index time series matched to climate records such as ERA5 or CRU.

section: Effects of climate
label: Competitors decline poleward, so climate acts more directly there
measurable_quantities: species richness along latitude and elevation; frequency of stunted growth forms; relative importance of abiotic versus biotic range limits
candidate_data: GBIF and BIEN occurrence data for richness gradients, sPlot vegetation plots and TRY plant height data along gradients, with climate layers such as WorldClim or CHELSA.

section: Effects of climate
label: Climate limits species mainly indirectly, by favouring competitors
measurable_quantities: fraction of cultivated exotic species that naturalise; climatic match between cultivation sites and native range; establishment success with and without competitors or herbivores
candidate_data: GloNAF naturalised-flora data compared with horticultural species lists and climate-niche data from GBIF and WorldClim, plus competitor- and herbivore-removal experiments.

section: Protection from the number of individuals
label: Many species need a large local stock to persist
measurable_quantities: per-capita survival or seed loss versus local population size; minimum viable population density; local abundance of rare species where present
candidate_data: Published Allee-effect and predator-satiation studies, and population time series in the Global Population Dynamics Database and COMPADRE.

section: Complex relations of all animals and plants throughout nature
label: Balanced struggles keep communities uniform over long periods
measurable_quantities: temporal turnover in species composition; variance in relative abundances over time; community stability metrics
candidate_data: Long-term community time series in BioTIME, the US LTER network, and pollen records from the Neotoma Paleoecology Database.

section: Complex relations of all animals and plants throughout nature
label: Chains of interaction link distant species' abundances
measurable_quantities: predator density; rodent density; bumblebee nest density; seed set and abundance of bee-pollinated plants
candidate_data: Interaction-network data (GloBI, Web of Life), published trophic-cascade field studies, and bumblebee and plant monitoring data from GBIF.

section: Struggle for life most severe between individuals and varieties of the same species; often severe between species of the same genus
label: Struggle is most severe between members of the same species
measurable_quantities: strength of intraspecific versus interspecific competition coefficients; per-capita effects of conspecific versus heterospecific density on growth or survival
candidate_data: Meta-analyses of competition experiments and plant neighbourhood data such as ForestGEO census plots that estimate conspecific versus heterospecific density effects.

section: Struggle for life most severe between individuals and varieties of the same species; often severe between species of the same genus
label: Congeners compete more severely than species of different genera
measurable_quantities: competition strength versus phylogenetic distance; trait similarity versus relatedness; displacement of one species by a congener
candidate_data: Pairwise competition experiments related to phylogenies from Open Tree of Life or TimeTree, and co-occurrence data from sPlot or GBIF.

section: The relation of organism to organism the most important of all relations
label: Each organism's structure is shaped by its relations to other organisms
measurable_quantities: trait variation explained by biotic versus abiotic factors; trait shifts in response to competitors, predators or prey
candidate_data: Trait databases (TRY, AVONET) combined with interaction data (GloBI) and published character-displacement studies.

section: The relation of organism to organism the most important of all relations
label: Few species reach range edges where climate alone kills them
measurable_quantities: proportion of range limits set by abiotic tolerance versus biotic interactions; performance of transplants beyond range edges with and without competitors
candidate_data: Published transplant experiments beyond range limits, together with GBIF occurrence data and physiological tolerance compilations such as GlobTherm.

section: Natural Selection: its power compared with man’s selection, its power on characters of trifling importance, its power at all ages and on both sexes
label: Natural selection preserves favourable and destroys injurious variations
measurable_quantities: selection differentials and gradients on traits; heritability of traits; differential survival and reproduction
candidate_data: Compilations of selection gradients measured in wild populations, long-term field studies of wild populations, and experimental-evolution datasets such as the LTEE.

section: Natural Selection: its power compared with man’s selection, its power on characters of trifling importance, its power at all ages and on both sexes
label: Neutral variations escape selection and remain fluctuating
measurable_quantities: fitness effect of a character; variance of the character within and among populations; temporal fluctuation of character frequencies
candidate_data: Long-term studies of polymorphism frequencies in wild populations and morphological trait variance in trait databases, compared with measured selection on those traits.

section: Natural Selection: its power compared with man’s selection, its power on characters of trifling importance, its power at all ages and on both sexes
label: No native biota is so well adapted that it cannot be improved
measurable_quantities: number and share of established alien species per region; displacement of native species by aliens
candidate_data: Global alien-species databases such as GloNAF, the Alien Species First Records Database, and GRIIS (Global Register of Introduced and Invasive Species).

section: Natural Selection: its power compared with man’s selection, its power on characters of trifling importance, its power at all ages and on both sexes
label: Protective colours matching backgrounds are maintained by selection
measurable_quantities: background matching of coloration; predation rate on matching versus mismatching morphs; coloration versus habitat across species
candidate_data: Field predation experiments on cryptic versus conspicuous prey models, comparative plumage-colour datasets from museum specimens, and long-term morph-frequency records such as those for the peppered moth.

section: Natural Selection: its power compared with man’s selection, its power on characters of trifling importance, its power at all ages and on both sexes
label: Natural selection can modify organisms at any age
measurable_quantities: selection on juvenile versus adult traits; trait correlations between life stages; stage-specific heritability
candidate_data: Studies of stage-specific selection and morphological decoupling between larvae and adults in insects and amphibians, with phylogenies from Open Tree of Life.

section: Sexual Selection
label: Males of polygamous species fight most and carry special weapons
measurable_quantities: mating system (degree of polygyny); male weapon size or presence; sexual size dimorphism; intensity of male-male combat
candidate_data: Comparative mating-system and morphology data such as PanTHERIA, AVONET and published sexual-dimorphism compilations, analysed on phylogenies from BirdTree or VertLife.

section: Sexual Selection
label: Female choice over many generations can produce male ornaments
measurable_quantities: female preference for male song or plumage traits; mating success versus ornament expression; ornament evolution across lineages
candidate_data: Mate-choice experiments and field mating-success studies in birds, together with plumage and song comparative datasets analysed on BirdTree phylogenies.

section: Sexual Selection
label: Sex differences in species with shared habits are mainly sexually selected
measurable_quantities: degree of sexual dimorphism; measures of sexual selection intensity (mating system, variance in male mating success); ecological differences between sexes
candidate_data: Comparative sexual-dimorphism and mating-system data (e.g. AVONET, PanTHERIA, published bird plumage dichromatism scores) analysed on phylogenies.

section: Natural Selection: its power compared with man’s selection, its power on characters of trifling importance, its power at all ages and on both sexes
label: Flowers and their insect visitors become mutually adapted
measurable_quantities: corolla tube length; pollinator proboscis length; trait matching across plant-pollinator pairs; pollination success versus trait match
candidate_data: Plant-pollinator interaction networks (Web of Life, GloBI) with floral and pollinator trait data, and published studies on correlated tube and tongue lengths.

section: Natural Selection: its power compared with man’s selection, its power on characters of trifling importance, its power at all ages and on both sexes
label: Natural selection works only by accumulating very small modifications
measurable_quantities: distribution of effect sizes of adaptive changes; rates of morphological change between successive generations or fossil samples
candidate_data: Experimental-evolution datasets (e.g. LTEE) and fine-scale fossil sequences in the Paleobiology Database that record morphological change over time.

section: On the generality of intercrosses between individuals of the same species
label: Crossing increases vigour; close interbreeding decreases it
measurable_quantities: offspring survival and fertility from outcrosses versus inbred matings; inbreeding depression; heterosis
candidate_data: Meta-analyses of inbreeding depression and heterosis in wild and domestic populations, and pedigreed long-term wild-population and livestock breeding records.

section: On the generality of intercrosses between individuals of the same species
label: No organism self-fertilises indefinitely; occasional crosses are needed
measurable_quantities: outcrossing rate; persistence and diversification rate of selfing or asexual lineages; longevity of exclusively selfing lineages
candidate_data: Plant mating-system compilations (outcrossing-rate databases in the literature), phylogenetic studies of selfing and asexual lineage age using TimeTree or Open Tree of Life.

section: On the generality of intercrosses between individuals of the same species
label: Trees more often have separate sexes than other plants
measurable_quantities: frequency of dioecy and monoecy in trees versus herbs; growth form
candidate_data: Plant sexual-system and growth-form data from the Tree of Sex database, TRY, and regional floras, analysed on Open Tree of Life phylogenies.

section: Circumstances favourable and unfavourable to Natural Selection, namely, intercrossing, isolation, number of individuals
label: Large populations favour natural selection by supplying more variations
measurable_quantities: population size; rate of adaptation; rate of appearance of beneficial variants
candidate_data: Experimental-evolution studies that manipulate population size (e.g. microbial evolution datasets deposited in Dryad) and comparative studies of adaptation rate versus population size.

section: Circumstances favourable and unfavourable to Natural Selection, namely, intercrossing, isolation, number of individuals
label: Large areas produce more, faster-forming and wider-spreading new species
measurable_quantities: speciation or diversification rate versus area; range size and spread of lineages originating in large versus small areas
candidate_data: Dated phylogenies (TimeTree, BirdTree) combined with biogeographic range data (GBIF, IUCN range maps) to estimate diversification rates by region area.

section: Circumstances favourable and unfavourable to Natural Selection, namely, intercrossing, isolation, number of individuals
label: Freshwater biotas evolve and go extinct more slowly, keeping relict forms
measurable_quantities: origination and extinction rates of freshwater versus marine or terrestrial lineages; frequency of relict (living-fossil) lineages by habitat
candidate_data: Paleobiology Database origination and extinction rates by environment, and dated fish phylogenies (e.g. Fish Tree of Life) for diversification by habitat.

section: Slow action
label: Natural selection acts slowly, intermittently and on few species at a time
measurable_quantities: rates of morphological change in fossil lineages; proportion of lineages changing in a given interval; evolutionary stasis versus change in fossil series
candidate_data: Fossil time series and occurrence data in the Paleobiology Database and Neotoma, and compilations of evolutionary rates across timescales.

section: Extinction caused by Natural Selection
label: Favoured forms make less favoured forms rare, and rarity precedes extinction
measurable_quantities: abundance or occupancy decline before extinction; abundance trends of competing species; extinction risk versus rarity
candidate_data: Paleobiology Database occupancy trajectories before extinction, IUCN Red List assessments, and the Living Planet Index abundance trends.

section: Extinction caused by Natural Selection
label: New forms press hardest on and tend to exterminate their nearest relatives
measurable_quantities: extinction of a lineage in relation to origination of close relatives; phylogenetic clustering of extinctions; replacement of older breeds or varieties by newer ones
candidate_data: Paleobiology Database origination and extinction data analysed for clade replacement, dated phylogenies (TimeTree), and historical records of livestock breed replacement such as FAO DAD-IS.

section: Divergence of Character, related to the diversity of inhabitants of any small area, and to naturalisation
label: Divergence of character maximises the life an area supports
measurable_quantities: species or genus richness per unit area; biomass or individual density per unit area
candidate_data: Plot-level biodiversity-productivity experiments (e.g. Cedar Creek BigBio, Jena Experiment); sPlot vegetation plots

section: Divergence of Character, related to the diversity of inhabitants of any small area, and to naturalisation
label: The closest-competing neighbours tend to belong to different genera and orders
measurable_quantities: genera-to-species and orders-to-species ratios in small plots versus regional pools; phylogenetic dispersion of local communities
candidate_data: Vegetation plot databases (sPlot, BIEN plots) with phylogenies from Open Tree of Life to compute phylogenetic over- or under-dispersion.

section: Divergence of Character, related to the diversity of inhabitants of any small area, and to naturalisation
label: Naturalised floras add proportionally more new genera than new species
measurable_quantities: proportion of naturalised species in genera absent from the native flora; species-to-genus ratio of naturalised versus native floras; phylogenetic distance of naturalised species to natives
candidate_data: GloNAF naturalised-flora checklists compared with native floras, with phylogenetic distances from Open Tree of Life.

section: Action of Natural Selection, through Divergence of Character and Extinction, on the descendants from a common parent
label: Intermediate forms and parent species tend to go extinct
measurable_quantities: persistence of ancestral morphotypes alongside descendants; frequency of budding versus anagenetic replacement in fossil lineages; survival of intermediate morphologies
candidate_data: Paleobiology Database occurrence data and published ancestor-descendant fossil series (e.g. planktonic foraminifera lineage data).

section: Action of Natural Selection, through Divergence of Character and Extinction, on the descendants from a common parent
label: Extinct species are often intermediate between living groups
measurable_quantities: morphological position of fossil taxa relative to living groups; phylogenetic placement of fossils (stem versus crown); disparity between groups through time
candidate_data: Paleobiology Database taxonomy, morphological character matrices in MorphoBank, and phylogenies including fossils in Open Tree of Life.

section: Summary
label: Differences between varieties grow into differences between species and genera
measurable_quantities: phenotypic divergence versus time since divergence; divergence of within-species varieties compared with between-species differences
candidate_data: Dated phylogenies (TimeTree) combined with trait data (AVONET, TRY) to relate trait divergence to divergence time, and fossil series in the Paleobiology Database.

section: Summary
label: Very few species of past periods have living descendants
measurable_quantities: fraction of species or clades in a past interval with living descendants; clade extinction rates; shape of phylogenies including fossils
candidate_data: Paleobiology Database occurrence and range data, combined with time-calibrated phylogenies from TimeTree and Open Tree of Life.

section: Effects of external conditions.
label: Variability is induced by changed conditions acting on the reproductive system
measurable_quantities: phenotypic variance of domesticated vs wild conspecifics; frequency of developmental abnormalities under captive vs wild conditions; variance in offspring traits after environmental change of parents
candidate_data: Comparative morphometric datasets of domestic breeds and their wild ancestors (e.g. dog and pigeon morphometrics on Dryad); plant common-garden and transplant experiments.

section: Effects of external conditions.
label: Direct effects of climate and food on organisms are small
measurable_quantities: magnitude of phenotypic plasticity in response to temperature or diet; plasticity effect sizes in animals vs plants
candidate_data: Meta-analytic datasets of phenotypic plasticity from reciprocal-transplant and common-garden experiments, many archived on Dryad; TRY plant trait database for within-species trait variation across environments.

section: Use and disuse, combined with natural selection; organs of flight and of vision.
label: Flightlessness of birds on predator-free oceanic islands is caused by disuse
measurable_quantities: incidence of flightlessness on islands with vs without mammalian predators; relative wing size in island vs mainland relatives
candidate_data: AVONET avian morphology database and bird phylogenies (BirdTree) for island vs mainland wing-length comparisons; subfossil records of extinct flightless island birds.

section: Use and disuse, combined with natural selection; organs of flight and of vision.
label: Wingless Madeira beetles result mainly from selection against being blown to sea
measurable_quantities: proportion of flightless insect species per island; wind exposure of islands; wing reduction in ground-feeding vs flower-feeding island insects
candidate_data: Island insect checklists with flight-capability traits (e.g. published datasets on flightlessness in island insects, including sub-Antarctic and Macaronesian faunas) combined with climate data on wind speed.

section: Use and disuse, combined with natural selection; organs of flight and of vision.
label: Blindness in cave animals results from disuse
measurable_quantities: rate of eye regression in cave vs surface lineages; energetic cost of eye tissue in darkness; signatures of selection on eye-related traits in cave populations
candidate_data: Cave fish (Astyanax mexicanus) comparative and experimental datasets; GenBank/SRA sequence data for cave and surface populations of cave-dwelling taxa.

section: Use and disuse, combined with natural selection; organs of flight and of vision.
label: Cave animals are related to surface fauna of their own continent
measurable_quantities: phylogenetic sister-group relationships of cave taxa; phylogenetic distance between cave taxa and local surface relatives vs cave taxa on other continents
candidate_data: Molecular phylogenies of cave beetles, amphipods and fish from GenBank and Open Tree of Life.

section: Acclimatisation.
label: Species ranges are limited by competition as much as by climate
measurable_quantities: climatic niche breadth of native range vs naturalised range; performance of species transplanted beyond range limits; range-limit position relative to climatic tolerance
candidate_data: GBIF occurrence records combined with WorldClim climate layers for native vs introduced ranges; GloNAF naturalised alien flora database; published transplant experiments beyond range limits.

section: Correlation of growth.
label: Homologous parts tend to vary together
measurable_quantities: phenotypic correlation between homologous vs non-homologous traits; covariation of fore- and hindlimb dimensions
candidate_data: Morphometric datasets of limb and skeletal measurements (e.g. mammal and bird skeletal datasets on Dryad and MorphoSource) analysed for morphological integration.

section: Correlation of growth.
label: Taxonomically important characters may be useless products of correlated growth
measurable_quantities: fitness effects of diagnostic characters; correlation of diagnostic characters with other developing structures
candidate_data: Plant trait databases (TRY) and phylogenies to test whether taxonomically diagnostic fruit or seed traits are correlated with adaptive traits; few direct datasets known.

section: Compensation and economy of growth.
label: Natural selection reduces superfluous parts without compensatory enlargement
measurable_quantities: rate of loss of unused structures in parasitic or sheltered lineages; correlation between reduction of one organ and enlargement of others
candidate_data: Phylogenetic comparative datasets on trait loss in parasites and cave or island lineages; experimental-evolution datasets (e.g. LTEE, Dryad) on loss of unused functions.

section: Multiple, rudimentary, and lowly organised structures variable.
label: Parts repeated many times in an individual are variable in number
measurable_quantities: within-species coefficient of variation in part counts; mean part count per individual
candidate_data: Vertebral count datasets for snakes and fishes and floral organ counts from herbarium and flora databases (e.g. published Dryad datasets on vertebral number variation).

section: Parts developed in an unusual manner are highly variable: specific characters more variable than generic: secondary sexual characters variable.
label: Parts unusually developed relative to congeners are highly variable
measurable_quantities: within-species coefficient of variation of a trait; deviation of species trait mean from congeneric mean
candidate_data: Museum morphometric datasets for congeneric species (e.g. AVONET for birds) allowing comparison of trait variance against trait exaggeration relative to congeners.

section: Parts developed in an unusual manner are highly variable: specific characters more variable than generic: secondary sexual characters variable.
label: Specific characters are more variable than generic characters
measurable_quantities: intraspecific variance of species-diagnostic vs genus-diagnostic characters
candidate_data: Taxonomic character matrices (e.g. MorphoBank) combined with intraspecific morphometric data from museum collections.

section: Parts developed in an unusual manner are highly variable: specific characters more variable than generic: secondary sexual characters variable.
label: Congeners differ more in secondary sexual characters than in other parts
measurable_quantities: interspecific divergence in male ornament traits vs non-sexual traits; male vs female interspecific plumage divergence
candidate_data: Comparative plumage colour and ornament datasets for birds (e.g. published spectrophotometric plumage datasets on Dryad) with AVONET morphology and BirdTree phylogenies.

section: Reversions to long-lost characters.
label: Long-lost characters reappear through a tendency transmitted each generation
measurable_quantities: frequency of ancestral phenotypes (atavisms) among offspring of crosses between breeds; persistence of atavistic tendencies across generations
candidate_data: Pigeon and chicken breed crossing studies; experimental crosses archived on Dryad; none known as a single comprehensive dataset.

section: Reversions to long-lost characters.
label: Horse, ass, hemionus, quagga and zebra descend from a striped common ancestor
measurable_quantities: monophyly of Equus; ancestral state reconstruction of striping; frequency of leg and shoulder stripes in horse breeds, asses and hybrids
candidate_data: Equid phylogenies from ancient and modern DNA in GenBank/SRA and Open Tree of Life; Paleobiology Database equid fossils; coat-pattern surveys of horse breeds.

section: Species of the same genus vary in an analogous manner.
label: Related species with shared constitution produce analogous variations
measurable_quantities: frequency of parallel variants across related species or breeds; phylogenetic signal in the occurrence of particular variants
candidate_data: Comparative data on parallel phenotypes in domestic breeds (pigeon, dog, chicken breed trait surveys) and phylogenetic studies of parallel evolution in wild taxa.

section: Absence or rarity of transitional varieties.
label: Formation of a new form exterminates its parent and transitional varieties
measurable_quantities: survival of ancestral or intermediate lineages after speciation; frequency of extant paraphyletic ancestral species
candidate_data: Paleobiology Database lineage durations and ancestor-descendant fossil series; molecular phylogenies from Open Tree of Life for budding vs replacement speciation patterns.

section: Absence or rarity of transitional varieties.
label: Zones of overlap between representative species are narrow
measurable_quantities: width of contact or hybrid zones relative to range size; abundance gradient toward range edges
candidate_data: GBIF occurrence data and range maps (e.g. IUCN/BirdLife range polygons) for parapatric sister species; published hybrid-zone width compilations.

section: Absence or rarity of transitional varieties.
label: Intermediate varieties are numerically rarer than the forms they connect
measurable_quantities: abundance of intermediate phenotypes or hybrids vs parental forms; area occupied by intermediate forms vs parental forms
candidate_data: Hybrid-zone and cline studies with genotype or phenotype frequency transects (many archived on Dryad); GBIF abundance and occurrence data for subspecies.

section: Absence or rarity of transitional varieties.
label: Common forms improve faster and supplant rare intermediate forms
measurable_quantities: rate of adaptation as a function of population size; persistence of small intermediate populations
candidate_data: Experimental-evolution datasets comparing adaptation rates across population sizes (e.g. microbial experiments on Dryad, LTEE-derived studies).

section: Transitions in habits of life.
label: Bat flight arose from an apparatus for gliding
measurable_quantities: ancestral state reconstruction of patagium configuration; morphology of early fossil bats
candidate_data: Paleobiology Database records of Eocene bats; mammal phylogenies from TimeTree and Open Tree of Life; MorphoSource fossil scans.

section: Species with habits widely different from those of their allies.
label: Habits can change without corresponding change of structure
measurable_quantities: mismatch between morphology and ecology across species; phylogenetic order of behavioural vs morphological shifts
candidate_data: AVONET morphology and EltonTraits foraging and habitat data combined with BirdTree phylogenies to detect ecomorphological mismatches.

section: Organs of extreme perfection.
label: Complex eyes can be built by selection through graded useful steps
measurable_quantities: range of eye complexity among living related taxa; phylogenetic ordering of eye structures
candidate_data: Comparative eye morphology across invertebrates in published phylogenetic studies; Open Tree of Life phylogenies for ancestral-state reconstruction.

section: Organs of extreme perfection.
label: Theory fails if a complex organ could not arise by slight steps
measurable_quantities: existence of documented intermediate stages for complex organs
candidate_data: Fossil series in the Paleobiology Database and comparative phylogenetic studies of organ evolution; none known as a single dataset.

section: Means of transition.
label: Lung-bearing vertebrates descend from an ancestor with a swimbladder
measurable_quantities: ancestral state of air-filled organs in bony fishes; phylogenetic position of lunged vs swimbladder-bearing lineages
candidate_data: Vertebrate phylogenies (TimeTree, Open Tree of Life) with comparative anatomy of lungs and swimbladders; Paleobiology Database early osteichthyan fossils.

section: Cases of difficulty.
label: Selection can independently produce similar organs in distantly related beings
measurable_quantities: number of independent origins of a trait on a phylogeny; structural differences between convergent organs
candidate_data: Fish phylogenies (Fish Tree of Life, Open Tree of Life) for mapping origins of electric organs; insect phylogenies for bioluminescence.

section: Natura non facit saltum.
label: Few organs lack any known transitional grade
measurable_quantities: proportion of organs with known intermediate states in living or fossil relatives
candidate_data: Comparative anatomical character matrices (MorphoBank) and fossil series in the Paleobiology Database.

section: Organs of small importance.
label: Most of an organism's structure is due to inheritance, not current use
measurable_quantities: phylogenetic signal of morphological traits; proportion of morphological variance explained by phylogeny vs ecology
candidate_data: Phylogenetic comparative analyses of morphology vs ecology using AVONET or mammal trait databases (e.g. PanTHERIA) with TimeTree phylogenies.

section: Organs of small importance.
label: No structure exists solely for the good of another species
measurable_quantities: fitness effect on the bearer of traits that benefit other species
candidate_data: Mutualism and plant-pollinator interaction studies measuring costs and benefits to each partner; none known as a single dataset.

section: Organs not in all cases absolutely perfect.
label: Selection makes organisms only as perfect as their local competitors
measurable_quantities: success of introduced species by region of origin; decline of native species after introductions
candidate_data: GloNAF and Global Register of Introduced and Invasive Species data on naturalisation success by donor region; Living Planet Index trends for island natives.

section: Organs of small importance.
label: Traits from laws of growth are later co-opted by descendants
measurable_quantities: phylogenetic timing of trait origin vs origin of its current function
candidate_data: Phylogenetic comparative datasets with ancestral-state reconstructions of trait and function (Open Tree of Life, TimeTree combined with trait matrices).

section: Natura non facit saltum.
label: Nature makes no leaps when past as well as present forms are included
measurable_quantities: morphological gaps between living taxa vs gaps when fossil taxa are included; rates of morphological change in fossil lineages
candidate_data: Paleobiology Database and morphological character matrices combining fossil and extant taxa (MorphoBank) to measure morphospace gaps.

section: The law of Unity of Type and of the Conditions of Existence embraced by the theory of Natural Selection.
label: Unity of type is explained by unity of descent
measurable_quantities: congruence between morphological similarity and molecular phylogeny
candidate_data: Molecular phylogenies from GenBank and Open Tree of Life compared with morphological character matrices (MorphoBank).

section: Instincts comparable with habits, but different in their origin
label: Instincts arise mainly by selection of accidental variations, not inherited habit
measurable_quantities: heritability of behavioural traits; response of behaviour to artificial selection; transgenerational effect of learned behaviour on offspring behaviour
candidate_data: Behavioural quantitative-genetics studies and artificial-selection experiments on behaviour (e.g. Drosophila and rodent selection lines, Dryad experimental-evolution datasets).

section: Instincts graduated
label: Complex instincts are reached by gradations visible in related species
measurable_quantities: behavioural character states mapped on phylogenies; number of intermediate behavioural states among related species
candidate_data: Phylogenetic comparative analyses of behaviour using trees from Open Tree of Life or TimeTree combined with published behavioural trait compilations.

section: Aphides and ants
label: No instinct exists for the exclusive good of another species
measurable_quantities: fitness benefit to the actor in interspecific mutualisms; fitness costs and benefits of tending for aphids with and without ants
candidate_data: Field and experimental studies of ant–aphid and other mutualisms measuring partner fitness; meta-analyses of mutualism costs and benefits.

section: Instincts variable
label: Instincts vary within species in a state of nature
measurable_quantities: intraspecific variation in migratory distance and direction; proportion of resident versus migratory individuals; variation in nest form within species
candidate_data: Bird tracking data (Movebank), bird ringing recoveries, and nest-record schemes such as the BTO Nest Record Scheme.

section: Instincts variable
label: Fear of man is acquired slowly by animals exposed to human persecution
measurable_quantities: flight initiation distance; time since human colonisation; hunting pressure; body size
candidate_data: Published comparative datasets of bird flight initiation distances across islands and mainland regions combined with human-settlement history.

section: Domestic instincts, their origin
label: Domestic instincts arise from habit and from human selection of chance variations
measurable_quantities: heritability of breed-specific behaviours; behavioural differences between domestic breeds and wild ancestors; response to selection for tameness
candidate_data: Dog breed behavioural survey data (e.g. C-BARQ) linked to breed genomic data, and long-term fox tameness selection experiments.

section: Natural instincts of the cuckoo, ostrich, and parasitic bees
label: Cuckoo brood parasitism evolved from occasional laying in other birds’ nests
measurable_quantities: phylogenetic distribution of nest-building and parasitic habits in Cuculidae; frequency of facultative intraspecific or interspecific egg dumping in related taxa
candidate_data: Cuckoo phylogenies (Open Tree of Life, TimeTree) combined with published compilations of breeding habits for ancestral-state reconstruction.

section: Slave-making ants
label: Slave-making in ants arose from capturing pupae as food
measurable_quantities: phylogenetic relationships of slave-making ants and their hosts; degree of dependence on slaves across species; predation on pupae of other ant species by non-slave-making ants
candidate_data: Ant phylogenies and natural-history records (AntWeb, AntWiki, Open Tree of Life) for comparative analysis of social parasitism.

section: Hive-bee, its cell-making instinct
label: Hive-bee comb building evolved by gradual modification of simpler bee instincts
measurable_quantities: cell shape and regularity across bee taxa; phylogenetic position of comb-building lineages; cell packing geometry
candidate_data: Published comparative measurements of nest architecture in Apidae combined with bee phylogenies (Open Tree of Life).

section: Hive-bee, its cell-making instinct
label: Hive-bee cells form by bees sweeping equal spheres and building at intersections
measurable_quantities: shape of newly built versus mature cells; spacing of working bees; wall thickness and angles of cells
candidate_data: Imaging and micro-CT studies of honeybee comb construction and cell geometry, and experimental comb-building studies.

section: Hive-bee, its cell-making instinct
label: The hive-bee comb is maximally economical of wax
measurable_quantities: wax per unit volume of storage; cell angles compared with mathematically optimal partitions; sugar consumed per unit wax secreted
candidate_data: Published geometric measurements of honeycomb cells and mathematical analyses of optimal space partitions; apicultural data on wax production costs.

section: Neuter or sterile insects
label: Selection on the family explains traits of sterile social-insect workers
measurable_quantities: colony-level fitness in relation to worker traits; heritability of worker traits through queens and males; relatedness within colonies
candidate_data: Social-insect genomic and colony-fitness studies, including published relatedness estimates and caste-trait heritability data.

section: Neuter or sterile insects
label: Neuter insects of one nest should show graded structural differences
measurable_quantities: within-nest distribution of worker size; allometry of head, jaw and ocelli among workers; frequency of intermediate morphs
candidate_data: Morphometric data on ant worker polymorphism from museum specimens (e.g. AntWeb imaging) and published allometry studies.

section: Neuter or sterile insects
label: Discrete worker castes arose by selection eliminating intermediate forms
measurable_quantities: degree of caste discreteness across related species; phylogenetic order of continuous versus discrete worker polymorphism
candidate_data: Ant phylogenies (Open Tree of Life, AntWeb) combined with comparative data on worker polymorphism for ancestral-state reconstruction.

section: Summary
label: Allied species in distant regions retain nearly the same instincts
measurable_quantities: phylogenetic signal in behavioural traits; behavioural similarity versus environmental similarity among congeners
candidate_data: Phylogenetic signal analyses of behavioural traits (e.g. nest construction) using bird phylogenies from Open Tree of Life or TimeTree.

section: Distinction between the sterility of first crosses and of hybrids
label: Sterility of first crosses differs from sterility of hybrids
measurable_quantities: seed or offspring set in interspecific crosses; pollen or sperm viability in hybrids
candidate_data: Published plant and animal crossing studies measuring pre-zygotic and post-zygotic isolation separately (e.g. Coyne and Orr’s Drosophila compilations).

section: Sterility various in degree, not universal, affected by close interbreeding, removed by domestication
label: Close interbreeding lowers fertility while occasional crossing raises it
measurable_quantities: fertility under inbreeding versus outbreeding; inbreeding depression coefficients; hybrid fertility across generations with and without inbreeding
candidate_data: Published meta-analyses of inbreeding depression in plants and animals and long-term pedigree datasets from zoos and livestock.

section: Sterility various in degree, not universal, affected by close interbreeding, removed by domestication
label: Hybrid sterility can be removed under domestication
measurable_quantities: number of wild ancestral species contributing to domestic forms; fertility of crosses between domestic forms of different wild origin; fertility of wild interspecific hybrids versus domestic descendants
candidate_data: Ancient and modern genomes of dogs, cattle and their wild relatives in GenBank/SRA documenting admixture, plus crossing records of zebu and taurine cattle.

section: Sterility various in degree, not universal, affected by close interbreeding, removed by domestication
label: Some sterility in crosses between species is very general but not universal
measurable_quantities: proportion of interspecific crosses showing reduced fertility; hybrid fertility relative to parental species
candidate_data: Compilations of reproductive isolation across species pairs (e.g. Coyne and Orr Drosophila data, plant crossing compilations) and hybrid zone studies.

section: Laws governing the sterility of hybrids
label: Difficulty of first cross and sterility of hybrids correspond only loosely
measurable_quantities: crossing success of first crosses; fertility of resulting hybrids; correlation between the two across species pairs
candidate_data: Reproductive-isolation compilations recording both pre-zygotic and post-zygotic isolation for the same species pairs (e.g. Coyne and Orr Drosophila data).

section: Laws governing the sterility of hybrids
label: Cross fertility is largely governed by systematic affinity
measurable_quantities: crossability and hybrid fertility versus phylogenetic or genetic distance between parent species
candidate_data: Compilations of reproductive isolation versus genetic distance (e.g. Coyne and Orr Drosophila data and analogous plant and bird datasets) with divergence times from TimeTree.

section: Laws governing the sterility of hybrids
label: Reciprocal crosses between the same two species often differ greatly in success
measurable_quantities: seed set or offspring number in each direction of reciprocal crosses; hybrid fertility from each reciprocal cross
candidate_data: Published plant crossing compilations reporting reciprocal-cross asymmetry in hybrid viability and fertility.

section: Sterility not a special endowment, but incidental on other differences
label: Cross sterility is incidental on reproductive differences, not specially endowed
measurable_quantities: accumulation of reproductive isolation with divergence time; evidence of direct selection for isolation versus by-product divergence
candidate_data: Comparative studies of the rate of accumulation of reproductive isolation with divergence time (TimeTree divergence estimates with crossing data) and genetic studies of hybrid incompatibility loci.

section: Causes of the sterility of first crosses and of hybrids
label: Early embryo death is a frequent cause of sterility in first crosses
measurable_quantities: fertilisation rate versus hatching or germination rate in interspecific crosses; stage of embryonic mortality
candidate_data: Published bird and plant hybridisation studies recording fertilisation and embryo mortality separately (e.g. avian hybrid egg-viability studies, endosperm-failure studies in plants).

section: Causes of the sterility of first crosses and of hybrids
label: Hybrid sterility resembles sterility caused by unnatural conditions
measurable_quantities: fertility of hybrids versus general vigour; fertility of captive or cultivated species versus wild conspecifics; sex-specific impairment of fertility
candidate_data: Zoo breeding records (e.g. Species360 ZIMS) for captive fertility and published hybrid fertility and vigour measurements.

section: Parallelism between the effects of changed conditions of life and crossing
label: Slight changes of conditions and slight crosses both increase vigour and fertility
measurable_quantities: offspring fitness as a function of genetic distance between parents; fitness under small environmental changes versus constant conditions
candidate_data: Published studies of optimal outcrossing distance and heterosis versus outbreeding depression in plants and animals.

section: Fertility of varieties when crossed and of their mongrel offspring not universal
label: Fertility of crossed varieties is not universal nor a species criterion
measurable_quantities: seed set or offspring number in crosses between varieties of one species; fertility of mongrel offspring
candidate_data: Crop germplasm crossing records and studies of intraspecific reproductive isolation (e.g. maize gametophyte factor studies, intraspecific crossing in Arabidopsis).

section: Hybrids and mongrels compared independently of their fertility
label: Hybrids vary little in the first generation but greatly in later generations
measurable_quantities: phenotypic variance in first-generation versus later-generation hybrids
candidate_data: Published crossing experiments comparing trait variance in F1 and F2 or later hybrid generations in plants and animals.

section: Hybrids and mongrels compared independently of their fertility
label: Apart from fertility, offspring of crossed species and crossed varieties are alike
measurable_quantities: parental resemblance of offspring; variability across generations; rates of reversion in backcrosses
candidate_data: Published comparative crossing studies of inter- and intraspecific crosses in plants and animals.

section: Summary
label: No fundamental distinction exists between species and varieties
candidate_data: none known

section: On the nature of extinct intermediate varieties; on their number
label: Extinct intermediates connect each species to a common progenitor, not to each other
measurable_quantities: morphological character states of fossil taxa relative to living sister taxa; frequency with which fossils are directly intermediate versus ancestral-like with unique characters
candidate_data: Morphological character matrices from phylogenetic studies (e.g. MorphoBank) combined with dated fossil occurrences in the Paleobiology Database.

section: On the nature of extinct intermediate varieties; on their number
label: The number of past intermediate and transitional links was inconceivably great
measurable_quantities: estimated total number of species that have ever lived; ratio of extinct to living species
candidate_data: Diversity-through-time estimates from the Paleobiology Database and time-calibrated phylogenies such as TimeTree and Open Tree of Life.

section: On the vast lapse of time, as inferred from the rate of deposition and of denudation
label: Denudation of the Weald implies roughly 300 million years since the late Chalk
measurable_quantities: age of the late Chalk / end of the Secondary period in years; coastal cliff retreat rates
candidate_data: Radiometrically calibrated geological time scale (International Commission on Stratigraphy chart) and published coastal cliff retreat rate measurements.

section: On the poorness of our palæontological collections
label: Soft-bodied organisms and remains on non-depositing sea floor are not preserved
measurable_quantities: proportion of living taxa with mineralised versus soft bodies represented in the fossil record; fossil occurrence frequency versus sedimentation rate
candidate_data: Paleobiology Database occurrence data compared with living taxonomic inventories (e.g. WoRMS), plus taphonomic experiment literature.

section: On the intermittence of geological formations
label: Successive formations are separated by wide intervals of unrecorded time
measurable_quantities: duration of unconformities and hiatuses relative to deposited intervals; stratigraphic completeness by time resolution
candidate_data: Radiometrically dated stratigraphic sections and gap-bound sedimentary package compilations (e.g. Macrostrat).

section: On the intermittence of geological formations
label: Thick fossil-rich formations accumulate during subsidence
measurable_quantities: subsidence rate during deposition of fossiliferous units; fossil abundance versus sediment accumulation and subsidence history
candidate_data: Macrostrat sedimentary column data with backstripped subsidence histories, combined with Paleobiology Database occurrences.

section: On the intermittence of geological formations
label: Speciation peaks during elevation, but fossil deposits form mainly during subsidence
measurable_quantities: origination and extinction rates versus sea-level / subsidence phase; volume of preserved fossiliferous sediment by tectonic phase
candidate_data: Paleobiology Database origination/extinction rates compared with Macrostrat rock-volume and sea-level reconstructions.

section: On the absence of intermediate varieties in any one formation
label: A single formation is likely shorter than the time needed to transform a species
measurable_quantities: duration of geological formations in years; mean fossil species duration
candidate_data: Formation age ranges from Macrostrat and species longevity estimates from the Paleobiology Database.

section: On the absence of intermediate varieties in any one formation
label: First appearance of a species in a formation usually marks immigration
measurable_quantities: diachroneity of first appearances of the same species across regions; fraction of local first appearances preceded by earlier occurrences elsewhere
candidate_data: Paleobiology Database occurrences with stratigraphic ages, compared across regions; Neptune database for marine microfossils.

section: On the absence of intermediate varieties in any one formation
label: Only a few transitional links should be found, and these will be ranked as species
measurable_quantities: number of documented stratophenetic transitional series; frequency of fossil chronospecies splitting within lineages
candidate_data: Paleobiology Database taxonomic records and published high-resolution microfossil lineage series (e.g. Neptune foraminifera data).

section: On the sudden appearance of groups of species
label: Apparent sudden origin of groups reflects missing earlier records
measurable_quantities: change over time in the oldest known fossil age of major groups; gap between molecular divergence estimates and first fossil occurrences
candidate_data: Historical versus current first occurrences in the Paleobiology Database, and molecular divergence times from TimeTree.

section: On the sudden appearance of groups of species
label: After a key new way of life is acquired, many divergent forms arise quickly
measurable_quantities: diversification rate after origin of a key trait versus before; time from trait origin to group-wide radiation
candidate_data: Time-calibrated phylogenies (TimeTree, Open Tree of Life) with trait data, and Paleobiology Database diversity curves for groups such as birds, bats and pterosaurs.

section: On their sudden appearance in the lowest known fossiliferous strata
label: Long ages of abundant life preceded the lowest Silurian strata
measurable_quantities: age of oldest evidence of life; duration of Precambrian fossil record relative to Phanerozoic
candidate_data: Dated Precambrian fossil and biomarker records (microfossils, stromatolites, Ediacaran biota) compiled in the Paleobiology Database and the geological time scale.

section: On their sudden appearance in the lowest known fossiliferous strata
label: Oceans and continents have kept roughly their present positions since the Silurian
measurable_quantities: age of oceanic crust; palaeogeographic positions of continents through the Phanerozoic
candidate_data: Seafloor age grids from marine magnetic anomalies and plate reconstructions (e.g. GPlates / PALEOMAP), and ocean drilling (DSDP/ODP/IODP) cores.

section: On the slow and successive appearance of new species
label: New species have appeared slowly and successively on land and in the sea
measurable_quantities: distribution of first-appearance dates within and across stages; origination rates per interval
candidate_data: Paleobiology Database and Neptune species first occurrences with high-resolution age models.

section: On their different rates of change
label: Species of different genera and classes change at different rates
measurable_quantities: rates of morphological change per lineage; species turnover rates per clade
candidate_data: Paleobiology Database taxon durations by clade and morphological rate estimates from phylogenetic character data (e.g. MorphoBank) on TimeTree-dated trees.

section: On their different rates of change
label: Land organisms change faster than marine organisms
measurable_quantities: species or genus turnover rates in terrestrial versus marine clades; mean taxon durations by habitat
candidate_data: Paleobiology Database occurrence data split by environment, and NOW (New and Old Worlds) fossil mammal database for terrestrial turnover.

section: Species once lost do not reappear
label: A species that has gone extinct never reappears
measurable_quantities: frequency of true reappearance versus Lazarus taxa explained by sampling gaps
candidate_data: Paleobiology Database range-through and Lazarus-taxon analyses.

section: Groups of species follow the same general rules in their appearance and disappearance as do single species
label: A group's existence is continuous and it never reappears after disappearing
measurable_quantities: stratigraphic range continuity of genera and families; frequency of gaps in group ranges and their relation to sampling
candidate_data: Paleobiology Database genus ranges and Sepkoski's compendium of marine genera.

section: Groups of species follow the same general rules in their appearance and disappearance as do single species
label: Groups rise gradually in species number to a maximum, then gradually decline
measurable_quantities: species richness of a clade per time interval; shape of clade diversity trajectories (spindle diagrams)
candidate_data: Paleobiology Database clade diversity curves and clade-shape analyses.

section: On Extinction
label: Species and groups disappear gradually, place by place, not by global catastrophes
measurable_quantities: spatial and temporal pattern of last occurrences; proportion of extinction concentrated in mass-extinction events
candidate_data: Paleobiology Database last occurrences with geographic coordinates, and Neptune data for marine microfossils.

section: On Extinction
label: The extinction of a group is generally slower than its origination
measurable_quantities: asymmetry of clade diversity trajectories (centre of gravity); duration of rise versus decline phases
candidate_data: Paleobiology Database clade diversity trajectories and published clade-shape asymmetry analyses.

section: On Extinction
label: Rarity precedes extinction
measurable_quantities: abundance or occupancy trends before last occurrence; population declines before extinction
candidate_data: Paleobiology Database occurrence frequencies before last appearance, Living Planet Index population trends and IUCN Red List histories.

section: On Extinction
label: In later geological periods new species have roughly balanced extinctions
measurable_quantities: global diversity through time; origination versus extinction rates per interval
candidate_data: Paleobiology Database global diversity curves and origination/extinction rate estimates.

section: On Extinction
label: New descendants mainly exterminate their parent species and closest relatives
measurable_quantities: extinction rates of congeners as a function of diversification of a sister lineage; phylogenetic clustering of extinction
candidate_data: Paleobiology Database occurrences mapped onto phylogenies, and phylogenetic signal analyses of extinction risk using IUCN Red List and Open Tree of Life.

section: On simultaneous changes in the forms of life throughout the world
label: Marine forms of life change almost simultaneously throughout the world
measurable_quantities: synchrony of first and last appearances across regions; faunal similarity between contemporaneous distant assemblages
candidate_data: Paleobiology Database and Neptune occurrences with independent (radiometric or magnetostratigraphic) age control.

section: On the affinities of extinct species to each other and to living species
label: The more ancient a form, the more it differs from living forms
measurable_quantities: morphological distance from nearest living relative as a function of fossil age; proportion of extant genera in assemblages by age
candidate_data: Paleobiology Database (proportion of extant taxa by age) and morphological character matrices from MorphoBank.

section: On the affinities of extinct species to each other and to living species
label: Extinct forms fill gaps between existing genera, families and orders
measurable_quantities: placement of fossil taxa on phylogenies relative to living clades; reduction in branch lengths/gaps when fossils are included
candidate_data: Open Tree of Life and published total-evidence phylogenies combining fossil and living taxa (e.g. MorphoBank matrices).

section: On the affinities of extinct species to each other and to living species
label: Older members of distinct groups differ less from each other than living members
measurable_quantities: morphological distance between members of two groups as a function of geological age; number of diagnostic characters separating groups over time
candidate_data: Morphological disparity analyses on character matrices (e.g. MorphoBank) combined with Paleobiology Database ages.

section: On the affinities of extinct species to each other and to living species
label: Fossils from consecutive formations are more alike than those from remote ones
measurable_quantities: taxonomic similarity between assemblages as a function of time separation
candidate_data: Paleobiology Database assemblage data for faunal similarity-decay analyses.

section: On the state of development of ancient forms
label: Later faunas would outcompete earlier faunas under similar conditions
candidate_data: none known

section: On the succession of the same types within the same areas
label: Each region's fossils are succeeded by allied living forms in the same region
measurable_quantities: taxonomic affinity of regional late-Cenozoic fossils to living regional versus extra-regional faunas
candidate_data: Paleobiology Database and NOW fossil mammal database occurrences compared with living distributions in GBIF.

section: Present distribution cannot be accounted for by differences in physical conditions
label: Physical conditions do not explain the similarity or dissimilarity of regional biotas
measurable_quantities: compositional (taxonomic or phylogenetic) similarity between regions; climatic/environmental similarity between regions
candidate_data: Species occurrence data from GBIF and OBIS combined with WorldClim climate layers, and phylogenies from Open Tree of Life, allow partitioning biotic similarity into climatic and geographic/historical components.

section: Importance of barriers
label: Barriers to migration correspond closely to differences between regional biotas
measurable_quantities: species turnover (beta diversity) across barriers versus across equal distances without barriers; barrier type and estimated age
candidate_data: GBIF and OBIS occurrence records with biogeographic regionalisations (e.g. Holt et al. 2013 zoogeographic regions) and phylogenies from Open Tree of Life or TimeTree, including the well-studied trans-Isthmian marine species pairs.

section: Affinity of the productions of the same continent
label: Species of the same continent or sea are related despite differing stations
measurable_quantities: phylogenetic relatedness of co-continental species versus species from other continents in similar habitats
candidate_data: Phylogenies from Open Tree of Life or TimeTree combined with GBIF distributions allow testing whether species are phylogenetically clustered by continent more than by habitat or climate.

section: Affinity of the productions of the same continent
label: The bond linking inhabitants of the same area through space and time is inheritance
measurable_quantities: phylogenetic clustering of species by region; relatedness of fossil and living species from the same region
candidate_data: Dated phylogenies (TimeTree, Open Tree of Life) combined with fossil occurrences from the Paleobiology Database can test whether regional biotas form clades and whether fossil forms of a region are related to its living forms.

section: Affinity of the productions of the same continent
label: Migration or isolation alone does not cause modification
measurable_quantities: degree of phenotypic or taxonomic divergence after colonisation; change in the community of competitors experienced by colonists
candidate_data: Comparative studies of island and introduced populations, and experimental-evolution datasets (e.g. on Dryad) that manipulate community composition, could bear on it.

section: Centres of creation
label: Many genera are confined to one region and the most natural genera are local
measurable_quantities: proportion of taxa endemic to one region at each taxonomic rank; geographic range size of a genus versus the phylogenetic age or tightness of its species
candidate_data: GBIF distributions linked to taxonomic backbones and dated phylogenies (TimeTree, Open Tree of Life) allow measuring regional endemism by rank and its relation to clade age.

section: Centres of creation
label: Each species arose in a single area and spread from there
measurable_quantities: monophyly of conspecific populations across disjunct ranges; geographic origin inferred from phylogeographic structure
candidate_data: Phylogeographic sequence data in GenBank and population-genetic datasets on Dryad allow testing whether disjunct populations of a species share a single geographic origin.

section: Means of dispersal, by changes of climate and of the level of the land, and by occasional means
label: Continents and oceanic islands were not united by land in the recent period
measurable_quantities: bathymetric depth between islands and continents; geological age and origin (volcanic versus continental) of oceanic islands; past land connections reconstructed from sea-level history
candidate_data: GEBCO bathymetry, radiometric ages of oceanic islands from the geological literature, and plate-reconstruction and sea-level records bear directly on it.

section: Means of dispersal, by changes of climate and of the level of the land, and by occasional means
label: About a tenth of a flora's seeds could survive sea-drift across 900 miles
measurable_quantities: proportion of species whose diaspores float for a given duration; germination after sea-water immersion; ocean current speeds
candidate_data: Seed-buoyancy trait records (e.g. in the LEDA Traitbase) and published sea-water immersion experiments, combined with ocean-current data, could test the estimate.

section: Means of dispersal, by changes of climate and of the level of the land, and by occasional means
label: Occasional transport bridges hundreds of miles but not distant continents
measurable_quantities: frequency of long-distance dispersal events by distance; shared species between land masses as a function of separation distance
