candidate_data: Dated phylogenies (TimeTree) used to infer oceanic dispersal events, and island floras in GIFT (Global Inventory of Floras and Traits) against distance to source, could test it.

section: Dispersal during the Glacial period co-extensive with the world
label: Identical alpine species on distant mountains are relicts of the Glacial period
measurable_quantities: phylogeographic divergence times among mountain populations; fossil and pollen records of arctic species in now-temperate lowlands during glacials
candidate_data: Neotoma Paleoecology Database pollen and macrofossil records together with phylogeographic sequence data in GenBank for arctic-alpine species.

section: Dispersal during the Glacial period co-extensive with the world
label: North American and European temperate biotas share ancestry from Pliocene circumpolar land
measurable_quantities: divergence times of intercontinental sister taxa; fossil occurrences of shared taxa at high northern latitudes in the Pliocene and earlier Tertiary
candidate_data: Dated phylogenies from TimeTree and fossil occurrences from the Paleobiology Database can test the timing and high-latitude route of North American–European disjunctions.

section: Dispersal during the Glacial period co-extensive with the world
label: The Glacial period was simultaneous across the whole world
measurable_quantities: timing of glacial maxima in both hemispheres; paleotemperature records from tropical and polar regions
candidate_data: Ice-core records (e.g. EPICA Dome C), the LR04 benthic oxygen-isotope stack, and NOAA paleoclimate archives document the timing of glacial cooling worldwide.

section: Dispersal during the Glacial period co-extensive with the world
label: Plants of high mountains and temperate lowlands worldwide are identical or closely related
measurable_quantities: number of species and genera shared between northern temperate, tropical montane and southern temperate floras; phylogenetic relatedness of these floras
candidate_data: Plant occurrence and floristic data from GBIF, BIEN and GIFT combined with plant phylogenies from Open Tree of Life.

section: Dispersal during the Glacial period co-extensive with the world
label: Glacial interchange ran mainly north to south because northern forms were more dominant
measurable_quantities: number of north-to-south versus south-to-north dispersal events inferred from phylogenies; land area and population size of source regions
candidate_data: Biogeographic reconstructions on dated plant phylogenies (TimeTree, Open Tree of Life) with GBIF distributions can count the direction of inter-hemispheric dispersal events.

section: Dispersal during the Glacial period co-extensive with the world
label: Northern species naturalise far more often in the south than the reverse
measurable_quantities: number of species naturalised from Europe in South America and Australia; number of species naturalised from southern regions in Europe
candidate_data: The Global Naturalized Alien Flora (GloNAF) database and DAISIE European alien-species inventories record donor and recipient regions of naturalised species.

section: Dispersal during the Glacial period co-extensive with the world
label: Distinct southern genera spread from a once-vegetated Antarctica before the Glacial period
measurable_quantities: fossil plant occurrences in Antarctica; divergence times and inferred ancestral areas of southern disjunct clades
candidate_data: Antarctic fossil plant occurrences in the Paleobiology Database and dated phylogenies of southern clades (e.g. via TimeTree) bear on it.

section: Distribution of fresh-water productions
label: Fresh-water species range widely and allied species occur worldwide
measurable_quantities: geographic range size of fresh-water versus terrestrial species in the same groups; number of continents occupied by fresh-water genera
candidate_data: GBIF occurrence records and freshwater-specific compilations (e.g. Freshwater Ecoregions of the World, IUCN Red List freshwater assessments) can compare range sizes of aquatic and terrestrial taxa.

section: Distribution of fresh-water productions
label: Fresh-water fish species are not shared between distant continents
measurable_quantities: number of strictly fresh-water fish species native to more than one continent; species overlap between river basins within a continent
candidate_data: FishBase distribution records and global freshwater fish occurrence-by-drainage-basin compilations, together with GBIF, can test both parts.

section: Distribution of fresh-water productions
label: Water birds disperse seeds and eggs, explaining wide ranges of fresh-water life
measurable_quantities: frequency of viable propagules carried externally or internally by waterbirds; waterbird movement distances; genetic connectivity of aquatic populations along flyways
candidate_data: Waterbird tracking data in Movebank and published waterbird propagule-transport studies, with population-genetic data in GenBank or Dryad for aquatic plants and invertebrates.

section: On the inhabitants of oceanic islands
label: Oceanic islands have fewer species than equal continental areas
measurable_quantities: native species richness per unit area on oceanic islands versus continental samples of equal area
candidate_data: Island and mainland checklists in GIFT (Global Inventory of Floras and Traits) and GBIF allow species-area comparisons between oceanic islands and continental regions.

section: On the inhabitants of oceanic islands
label: Oceanic islands have a very high proportion of endemic species
measurable_quantities: proportion of endemic species on oceanic islands; endemic species per unit area on islands versus continents
candidate_data: GIFT island floras with endemism status, IUCN Red List and BirdLife range data for vertebrates, and GBIF occurrences.

section: On the inhabitants of oceanic islands
label: Island endemism is low in groups that arrive easily and in numbers
measurable_quantities: proportion of endemic species per taxonomic group on an island; dispersal ability or immigration frequency of each group
candidate_data: Island checklists with endemism status (GIFT, BirdLife, IUCN Red List) combined with dispersal traits (e.g. AVONET hand-wing index for birds) allow testing whether endemism declines with dispersal ability.

section: On the inhabitants of oceanic islands
label: Natural selection turns island herbaceous plants into shrubs and trees
measurable_quantities: frequency of derived woodiness in island versus mainland lineages; phylogenetic transitions from herbaceous to woody growth form
candidate_data: Global compilations of derived insular woodiness from the botanical literature, combined with plant phylogenies (Open Tree of Life) and growth-form data in the TRY plant trait database.

section: Absence of Batrachians and of terrestrial Mammals
label: Frogs, toads and newts are absent from oceanic islands
measurable_quantities: presence of native amphibian species on oceanic islands; establishment success of introduced amphibians on oceanic islands
candidate_data: AmphibiaWeb and IUCN Red List amphibian range maps, plus GBIF records and island geological origin, can test native amphibian occurrence on oceanic islands.

section: Absence of Batrachians and of terrestrial Mammals
label: No native terrestrial mammals on islands more than 300 miles from a continent
measurable_quantities: presence of native terrestrial mammals by island isolation distance; establishment of introduced mammals on remote islands
candidate_data: Native mammal ranges from PHYLACINE or IUCN Red List range maps, overlaid with island locations and distance to mainland.

section: Absence of Batrachians and of terrestrial Mammals
label: Bats occur on almost every island, often as endemic species
measurable_quantities: presence and number of native bat species on oceanic islands; proportion of island bat species that are endemic
candidate_data: IUCN Red List and PHYLACINE bat range data combined with island geography, and GBIF occurrence records.

section: Absence of Batrachians and of terrestrial Mammals
label: Sea depth between island and mainland predicts their mammalian affinity
measurable_quantities: depth of the channel between island and mainland; proportion of island mammal species shared with or congeneric with the mainland; island–mainland distance
candidate_data: GEBCO bathymetry combined with mammal ranges from PHYLACINE or IUCN Red List and a mammal phylogeny (e.g. via Open Tree of Life).

section: On the relation of the inhabitants of islands to those of the nearest mainland
label: Island endemics are related to species of the nearest continent
measurable_quantities: geographic location of the closest relatives (sister lineages) of island endemics; distance from island to the source region versus to the nearest continent
candidate_data: Phylogenies in Open Tree of Life and sequence data in GenBank, combined with GBIF distributions, allow identifying the source region of island endemic lineages.

section: On the relation of the inhabitants of islands to those of the nearest mainland
label: Species on islands of one archipelago are closest relatives of each other
measurable_quantities: phylogenetic relatedness among species on different islands of an archipelago versus to mainland species
candidate_data: Molecular phylogenies of archipelago radiations from GenBank and Open Tree of Life (e.g. Galapagos finches and mockingbirds).

section: On the relation of the inhabitants of islands to those of the nearest mainland
label: Naturalised species are usually not closely allied to the natives they join
measurable_quantities: phylogenetic distance between naturalised species and the native flora or fauna; proportion of naturalised species belonging to genera not native to the region
candidate_data: GloNAF naturalised-plant records combined with regional native floras (GIFT) and plant phylogenies (Open Tree of Life) allow direct tests.

section: On colonisation from the nearest source with subsequent modification
label: Inhabitants of any area are modified colonists from the most accessible source
measurable_quantities: phylogenetic relatedness of alpine, cave or lake species to species of surrounding lowlands versus distant similar habitats
candidate_data: Phylogenies from Open Tree of Life and GenBank sequences for alpine, cave and lake lineages, combined with GBIF distributions of their relatives.

section: On colonisation from the nearest source with subsequent modification
label: Regions sharing many allied species will also share some identical species
measurable_quantities: number of allied (congeneric) species shared between two regions; number of identical species shared between the same regions
candidate_data: GBIF occurrences or regional checklists (e.g. GIFT for plants) can measure the correlation between shared congeners and shared species across region pairs.

section: On colonisation from the nearest source with subsequent modification
label: The lower a group of organisms, the more widely it tends to range
measurable_quantities: geographic range size of species or genera by group; rate of morphological change by group; propagule size
candidate_data: GBIF occurrence-derived range sizes across major groups, with Paleobiology Database species durations as a proxy for rate of change.

section: Summary
label: Closer relatives tend to be closer together in time and space
measurable_quantities: phylogenetic distance between species pairs; geographic distance between their ranges; stratigraphic separation between fossil taxa
candidate_data: Dated phylogenies (TimeTree, Open Tree of Life) combined with GBIF range data and Paleobiology Database occurrences allow testing the correlation of phylogenetic with geographic and temporal distance.

section: CLASSIFICATION, groups subordinate to groups
label: Descent with divergence and extinction produces groups subordinate to groups
measurable_quantities: degree of hierarchical (tree-like) structure in character or sequence data; consistency of nested clades across independent character sets
candidate_data: Large phylogenies and their underlying character and sequence matrices (Open Tree of Life, GenBank, TreeBASE) allow tests of how tree-like the pattern of similarity is.

section: Natural system
label: The Natural System expresses propinquity of descent
measurable_quantities: congruence between traditional morphology-based classifications and independently inferred phylogenies
candidate_data: Comparison of traditional Linnaean taxonomies (e.g. Catalogue of Life, GBIF backbone) with phylogenies from Open Tree of Life.

section: Rules and difficulties in classification, explained on the theory of descent with modification
label: Characters least modified by adaptation are most constant and useful in classification
measurable_quantities: homoplasy or consistency index of characters; association between a character's ecological/functional relevance and its homoplasy
candidate_data: Published morphological character matrices (MorphoBank, TreeBASE) analysed on reference phylogenies to compare homoplasy of habit-related versus other characters.

section: Rules and difficulties in classification, explained on the theory of descent with modification
label: Higher taxonomic ranks are almost arbitrary
measurable_quantities: variation in crown or stem age of taxa of the same rank; variation in species richness and disparity among taxa of the same rank
candidate_data: Divergence times of genera, families and orders across groups from TimeTree, with taxonomy from the Catalogue of Life or GBIF backbone.

section: Rules and difficulties in classification, explained on the theory of descent with modification
label: Branches equally related by descent can differ greatly in amount of modification
measurable_quantities: morphological disparity or rate of change among sister lineages of equal age; variation in evolutionary rates among lineages
candidate_data: Dated phylogenies (TimeTree, Open Tree of Life) combined with morphological matrices (MorphoBank) to compare rates of morphological change across sister clades.

section: Classification of varieties
label: Varieties form nested groups for the same reason species do
measurable_quantities: hierarchical clustering of breeds or varieties; agreement between breed clustering and documented breed histories
candidate_data: Genome-wide population data for domestic breeds (e.g. dog, pigeon, cattle and chicken breed panels in GenBank/SRA) compared with recorded breed pedigrees.

section: Descent always used in classification
label: Characters shared across species with very different habits indicate common inheritance
measurable_quantities: phylogenetic signal of characters; fit of character distributions to a single origin versus multiple origins
candidate_data: Trait datasets mapped onto phylogenies (Open Tree of Life, TreeBASE, MorphoBank) to estimate the number of origins of widely shared characters.

section: Analogical or adaptive characters
label: Distinct lineages adapted to similar conditions converge in external form
measurable_quantities: frequency of convergent morphological evolution; mismatch between morphology-based groupings and phylogeny for habit-related traits
candidate_data: Phylogenies from Open Tree of Life combined with ecomorphological trait data (e.g. AVONET for birds, PanTHERIA for mammals) to quantify convergence among unrelated lineages.

section: CLASSIFICATION, groups subordinate to groups
label: Expanding dominant groups explain why all life falls into a few great classes
measurable_quantities: relationship between clade size and subsequent diversification rate; clade extinction rate as a function of clade size
candidate_data: Fossil occurrence data from the Paleobiology Database and dated molecular phylogenies (TimeTree) to test whether large clades grow and small clades disappear.

section: Affinities, general, complex and radiating
label: Aberrant groups are species-poor relicts of extinction
measurable_quantities: species richness of phylogenetically isolated lineages; branch length or evolutionary distinctiveness; fossil diversity history of relict clades
candidate_data: Evolutionary-distinctiveness scores computed on large phylogenies (Open Tree of Life, TimeTree) compared with clade species richness, plus Paleobiology Database records of past diversity of relict clades.

section: Affinities, general, complex and radiating
label: Affinities of one group to another are usually general, not to any single species
measurable_quantities: similarity of a taxon to each member of another group; phylogenetic position of taxa showing cross-group affinity (near the base of their group or not)
candidate_data: Morphological matrices (MorphoBank) and phylogenies (Open Tree of Life) to test whether taxa with cross-group affinities are early-diverging lineages.

section: Extinction separates and defines groups
label: Gaps between groups, even whole classes, are due to extinction of connecting forms
measurable_quantities: occurrence of fossil forms intermediate between currently distinct classes; morphological gap between groups before and after including fossil taxa
candidate_data: Paleobiology Database occurrences and published fossil character matrices (MorphoBank), e.g. for the dinosaur-to-bird transition.

section: MORPHOLOGY, between members of the same class, between parts of the same individual
label: Homologous parts change shape and size but keep the same relative connexions
measurable_quantities: frequency of changes in topological connectivity of homologous elements versus changes in shape and size
candidate_data: Comparative anatomical datasets and ontologies (e.g. Uberon, MorphoBank matrices) recording element connectivity across taxa.

section: MORPHOLOGY, between members of the same class, between parts of the same individual
label: Unity of type reflects a common progenitor's pattern modified by slight steps
measurable_quantities: presence of the shared pattern in early fossil members of the class; reconstructed ancestral states of homologous structures
candidate_data: Fossil occurrence and morphology data (Paleobiology Database, MorphoBank) for early members of classes, with ancestral-state reconstruction on Open Tree of Life phylogenies.

section: MORPHOLOGY, between members of the same class, between parts of the same individual
label: Serially homologous parts derive from many repeated similar elements in progenitors
measurable_quantities: number and similarity of serially repeated elements in early fossil members versus later members of each group
candidate_data: Paleobiology Database occurrences and fossil morphological matrices (MorphoBank) for early arthropods, vertebrates and seed plants.

section: EMBRYOLOGY, laws of, explained by variations not supervening at an early age, and being inherited at a corresponding age
label: Embryos of different animals in the same class are strikingly similar
measurable_quantities: morphological similarity of embryos across species by developmental stage; embryonic versus adult between-species divergence
candidate_data: Comparative embryo image and staging collections and published cross-species developmental time series (morphological and transcriptomic) for vertebrates and insects.

section: EMBRYOLOGY, laws of, explained by variations not supervening at an early age, and being inherited at a corresponding age
label: Active larvae are adapted to their own conditions as fully as adults
measurable_quantities: larval versus adult morphological divergence among allied species; association between larval ecology and larval morphology
candidate_data: Comparative larval and adult morphological datasets for marine invertebrates and insects mapped on phylogenies from Open Tree of Life.

section: EMBRYOLOGY, laws of, explained by variations not supervening at an early age, and being inherited at a corresponding age
label: Young of domestic breeds differ much less than adults
measurable_quantities: proportional differences between breeds at hatching or birth versus adulthood; ontogenetic allometric trajectories by breed
candidate_data: Published ontogenetic morphometric data for dog and pigeon breeds (e.g. skull growth series in museum collections and Dryad datasets).

section: EMBRYOLOGY, laws of, explained by variations not supervening at an early age, and being inherited at a corresponding age
label: Community of embryonic structure reveals community of descent
measurable_quantities: agreement between groupings based on embryonic/larval characters and independent phylogenies; agreement between adult-character groupings and independent phylogenies
candidate_data: Larval and adult morphological matrices (MorphoBank) compared against molecular phylogenies (Open Tree of Life, GenBank).

section: EMBRYOLOGY, laws of, explained by variations not supervening at an early age, and being inherited at a corresponding age
label: Ancient extinct forms should resemble the embryos of their living descendants
measurable_quantities: similarity of fossil adult morphology to embryonic versus adult morphology of living relatives
candidate_data: Fossil morphological data (Paleobiology Database, MorphoBank) combined with ontogenetic series of living relatives.

section: EMBRYOLOGY, laws of, explained by variations not supervening at an early age, and being inherited at a corresponding age
label: Embryological facts follow from late-appearing variations inherited at corresponding ages
measurable_quantities: developmental stage at which between-species differences first appear; divergence of developmental trajectories across ontogeny
candidate_data: Comparative ontogenetic morphometric series and cross-species developmental time series for vertebrates and insects.

section: RUDIMENTARY ORGANS; their origin explained
label: Rudimentary organs are extremely common throughout nature
measurable_quantities: proportion of taxa possessing vestigial structures; number of documented vestigial structures per clade
candidate_data: Comparative anatomical databases and ontologies (e.g. Uberon, Phenoscape) annotated for reduced or vestigial structures.

section: RUDIMENTARY ORGANS; their origin explained
label: Rudimentary organs are highly variable
measurable_quantities: within-species coefficient of variation of vestigial versus functional structures
candidate_data: Morphometric data on vestigial structures (e.g. cave-fish eyes, flightless-bird wings) in museum collections and Dryad datasets.

section: RUDIMENTARY ORGANS; their origin explained
label: Rudimentary organs are relatively larger in the embryo than in the adult
measurable_quantities: relative size of rudimentary organs across ontogenetic stages
candidate_data: Ontogenetic series and embryological descriptions of vestigial structures (e.g. whale and ruminant tooth germs, snake limb buds) in museum collections and literature.

section: RUDIMENTARY ORGANS; their origin explained
label: Disuse is the main cause of rudimentary organs
measurable_quantities: degree of organ reduction versus time since habitat change; evidence of reduction under relaxed versus active selection
candidate_data: Studies of cave-fish (Astyanax) and island flightless birds with dated phylogenies (TimeTree), plus experimental-evolution datasets in Dryad.

section: How far the theory of natural selection may be extended
label: Descent with modification embraces all members of each class
measurable_quantities: monophyly of classes in independent phylogenies; support for common ancestry within each class
candidate_data: Phylogenomic datasets and synthetic trees (Open Tree of Life, GenBank/SRA) testing monophyly and common ancestry of classes.

section: How far the theory of natural selection may be extended
label: Animals from at most four or five progenitors, plants from as many or fewer
measurable_quantities: number of independent origins of animals and of plants inferred from phylogenetic data
candidate_data: Phylogenomic data for animals and plants (GenBank/SRA, Open Tree of Life) testing monophyly of each kingdom versus multiple independent origins.

section: How far the theory of natural selection may be extended
label: All living things share chemical composition, cell structure and laws of growth
measurable_quantities: shared biochemical components and pathways across kingdoms; shared cellular structures across kingdoms
candidate_data: Cross-kingdom biochemical pathway and protein databases (KEGG, UniProt) documenting shared metabolism and cell components.

section: How far the theory of natural selection may be extended
label: Probably all organisms descend from one primordial form
measurable_quantities: statistical support for universal common ancestry versus multiple independent origins
candidate_data: Universally conserved sequence data (e.g. ribosomal RNA and protein sequences in GenBank, SILVA) used in formal tests of universal common ancestry.

section: Effects of its adoption on the study of Natural history
label: Species differ from varieties only in their intermediates having existed formerly
candidate_data: none known

section: Effects of its adoption on the study of Natural history
label: Organism-to-organism relations are the most important cause of organic change
measurable_quantities: relative explanatory power of biotic interactions (diversity, competitors) versus abiotic change (climate, sea level) for origination and extinction rates
candidate_data: Paleobiology Database occurrence data analysed together with paleoclimate and sea-level records.

section: Effects of its adoption on the study of Natural history
label: Amount of fossil change between formations measures elapsed time
measurable_quantities: faunal turnover between successive units; radiometrically dated time intervals between units
candidate_data: Paleobiology Database occurrences with ages from the Geologic Time Scale to correlate taxonomic turnover with absolute elapsed time.

section: Effects of its adoption on the study of Natural history
label: Rate of organic change was slower early in life's history
measurable_quantities: origination and extinction rates through time; rates of morphological change in early versus later clades; relationship between standing diversity and rate of change
candidate_data: Paleobiology Database diversity and turnover curves through the Phanerozoic, plus Precambrian microfossil and dated-phylogeny data (TimeTree).

section: Effects of its adoption on the study of Natural history
label: Known geological history is a fragment of the time since the first organism
measurable_quantities: age of the earliest evidence of life; age of the base of the Silurian/Cambrian fossil record
candidate_data: Radiometric ages from the Geologic Time Scale, Precambrian fossil records (Paleobiology Database) and molecular-clock estimates (TimeTree).

section: Effects of its adoption on the study of Natural history
label: Every mental power was acquired by gradation
measurable_quantities: distribution of cognitive abilities across related species; phylogenetic signal in cognitive traits
candidate_data: Comparative cognition datasets across primates and other animals (e.g. ManyPrimates), mapped on Open Tree of Life phylogenies.

section: Concluding remarks
label: Few living species will leave descendants; common species of dominant groups will prevail
measurable_quantities: survival and origination probability versus geographic range size and abundance; survival versus size of the higher group
candidate_data: Paleobiology Database occurrence data to relate past range size and clade size to lineage survival and production of daughter taxa.

section: Concluding remarks
label: Succession by generation has never been broken by a world-wide cataclysm
measurable_quantities: continuity of lineages across mass-extinction boundaries; proportion of lineages surviving each extinction event
candidate_data: Paleobiology Database records across mass-extinction boundaries and dated phylogenies (TimeTree) showing lineages crossing them.

section: Concluding remarks
label: Natural selection makes endowments tend towards perfection
measurable_quantities: long-term trends in measures of adaptation or fitness
candidate_data: Long-term experimental evolution of fitness (LTEE) and long-run fossil trends in the Paleobiology Database bear on part of the claim.

section: Concluding remarks
label: The 'entangled bank' laws produce the diversity of living forms
measurable_quantities: heritability of traits; standing variation; reproductive excess and mortality; selection differentials; rates of divergence and extinction
candidate_data: Experimental-evolution datasets (LTEE, Dryad), long-term wild-population studies, and Paleobiology Database diversification data each address components of the claim.
